When the flowers droop in the evening and cattle come back to their stalls, you stealthily come to my side and speak words that I do not understand. Is this how you must woo and win me with the opiate of drowsy murmur and cold kisses, O Death, my Death?

Will there be no proud ceremony for our wedding? Will you not tie up with a wreath your tawny coiled locks? Is there none to carry your banner before you, and will not the night be on fire with your red torch-lights, O Death, my Death?

Come with your conch-shells sounding, come in the sleepless night. Dress me with a crimson mantle, grasp my hand and take me. Let your chariot be ready at my door with your horses neighing impatiently. Raise my veil and look at my face proudly, O Death, my Death!
work: The Gardener, 81 · translated by the author

title: Fruit-Gathering · LXXXI
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
You, in your timeless watch, listen to my approaching steps while your gladness gathers in the morning twilight and breaks in the burst of light.

The nearer I draw to you the deeper grows the fervour in the dance of the sea.

Your world is a branching spray of light filling your hands, but your heaven is in my secret heart; it slowly opens its buds in shy love.
work: Fruit-Gathering, LXXXI · translated by the author

title: Look back on time with kindly eyes
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Look back on time with kindly eyes,
He doubtless did his best;
How softly sinks his trembling sun
In human nature's west!
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · VIII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 82
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Let life be beautiful like summer flowers and death like autumn leaves.
work: Stray Birds, 82 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 82
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
Time is endless in thy hands, my lord. There is none to count thy minutes.

Days and nights pass and ages bloom and fade like flowers. Thou knowest how to wait.

Thy centuries follow each other perfecting a small wild flower.

We have no time to lose, and having no time we must scramble for a chances. We are too poor to be late.

And thus it is that time goes by while I give it to every querulous man who claims it, and thine altar is empty of all offerings to the last.

At the end of the day I hasten in fear lest thy gate to be shut; but I find that yet there is time.
work: Gitanjali, 82 · translated by the author

title: The Gardener · 82
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: We are to play the game of death to-night, my bride and I. The night is black, the clouds in the sky are capricious, and the waves are raving at sea. We have left our bed of dreams, flung open the door and come out, my bride and I. We sit upon a swing, and the storm winds give us a wild push from behind. My bride starts up with fear and delight, she trembles and clings to my breast. Long have I served her tenderly. I made for her a bed of flowers and I closed the doors to shut out the rude light from her eyes. I kissed her gently on her lips and whispered softly in her ears till she half swooned in languor. She was lost in the endless mist of vague sweetness. She answered not to my touch, my songs failed to arouse her. To-night has come to us the call of the storm from the wild. My bride has shivered and stood up, she has clasped my hand and come out. Her hair is flying in the wind, her veil is fluttering, her garland rustles over her breast. The push of death has swung her into life. We are face to face and heart to heart, my bride and I.
work: The Gardener, 82 · translated by the author

title: Fruit-Gathering · LXXXII
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
I will utter your name, sitting alone among the shadows of my silent thoughts.

I will utter it without words, I will utter it without purpose.

For I am like a child that calls its mother an hundred times, glad that it can say "Mother."
work: Fruit-Gathering, LXXXII · translated by the author

title: A train went through a burial gate
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
A train went through a burial gate,
A bird broke forth and sang,
And trilled, and quivered, and shook his throat
Till all the churchyard rang;

And then adjusted his little notes,
And bowed and sang again.
Doubtless, he thought it meet of him
To say good-by to men.
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · IX · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 83
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: He who wants to do good knocks at the gate; he who loves finds the gate open.
work: Stray Birds, 83 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 83
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
Mother, I shall weave a chain of pearls for thy neck with my tears of sorrow.

The stars have wrought their anklets of light to deck thy feet, but mine will hang upon thy breast.

Wealth and fame come from thee and it is for thee to give or to withhold them. But this my sorrow is absolutely mine own, and when I bring it to thee as my offering thou rewardest me with thy grace.
work: Gitanjali, 83 · translated by the author

title: The Gardener · 83
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
She dwelt on the hillside by the edge of a maize-field, near the spring that flows in laughing rills through the solemn shadows of ancient trees. The women came there to fill their jars, and travellers would sit there to rest and talk. She worked and dreamed daily to the tune of the bubbling stream.

One evening the stranger came down from the cloud-hidden peak; his locks were tangled like drowsy snakes. We asked in wonder, "Who are you?" He answered not but sat by the garrulous stream and silently gazed at the hut where she dwelt. Our hearts quaked in fear and we came back home when it was night.

Next morning when the women came to fetch water at the spring by the _deodar_ trees, they found the doors open in her hut, but her voice was gone and where was her smiling face? The empty jar lay on the floor and her lamp had burnt itself out in the corner. No one knew where she had fled to before it was morning--and the stranger had gone.

In the month of May the sun grew strong and the snow melted, and we sat by the spring and wept. We wondered in our mind, "Is there a spring in the land where she has gone and where she can fill her vessel in these hot thirsty days?" And we asked each other in dismay, "Is there a land beyond these hills where we live?"

It was a summer night; the breeze blew from the south; and I sat in her deserted room where the lamp stood still unlit. When suddenly from before my eyes the hills vanished like curtains drawn aside. "Ah, it is she who comes. How are you, my child? Are you happy? But where can you shelter under this open sky? And, alas, our spring is not here to allay your thirst."

"Here is the same sky," she said, "only free from the fencing hills,--this is the same stream grown into a river,--the same earth widened into a plain." "Everything is here," I sighed, "only we are not." She smiled sadly and said, "You are in my heart." I woke up and heard the babbling of the stream and the rustling of the _deodars_ at night.
work: The Gardener, 83 · translated by the author

title: Fruit-Gathering · LXXXIII
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
I

I feel that all the stars shine in me. The world breaks into my life like a flood.

The flowers blossom in my body. All the youthfulness of land and water smokes like an incense in my heart; and the breath of all things plays on my thoughts as on a flute.

II

When the world sleeps I come to your door.

The stars are silent, and I am afraid to sing.

I wait and watch, till your shadow passes by the balcony of night and I return with a full heart.

Then in the morning I sing by the roadside;

The flowers in the hedge give me answer and the morning air listens,

The travellers suddenly stop and look in my face, thinking I have called them by their names.

III

Keep me at your door ever attending to your wishes, and let me go about in your Kingdom accepting your call.

Let me not sink and disappear in the depth of languor.

Let not my life be worn out to tatters by penury of waste.

Let not those doubts encompass me,--the dust of distractions.

Let me not pursue many paths to gather many things.

Let me not bend my heart to the yoke of the many.

Let me hold my head high in the courage and pride of being your servant.
work: Fruit-Gathering, LXXXIII · translated by the author

title: I died for beauty, but was scarce
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I died for beauty, but was scarce
Adjusted in the tomb,
When one who died for truth was lain
In an adjoining room.

He questioned softly why I failed?
"For beauty," I replied.
"And I for truth, -- the two are one;
We brethren are," he said.

And so, as kinsmen met a night,
We talked between the rooms,
Until the moss had reached our lips,
And covered up our names.
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · X · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 84
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: In death the many becomes one; in life the one becomes many. Religion will be one when God is dead.
work: Stray Birds, 84 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 84
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
It is the pang of separation that spreads throughout the world and gives birth to shapes innumerable in the infinite sky.

It is this sorrow of separation that gazes in silence all nights from star to star and becomes lyric among rustling leaves in rainy darkness of July.

It is this overspreading pain that deepens into loves and desires, into sufferings and joy in human homes; and this it is that ever melts and flows in songs through my poet’s heart.
work: Gitanjali, 84 · translated by the author

title: The Gardener · 84
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Over the green and yellow rice-fields sweep the shadows of the autumn clouds followed by the swift chasing sun. The bees forget to sip their honey; drunken with light they foolishly hover and hum. The ducks in the islands of the river clamour in joy for mere nothing. Let none go back home, brothers, this morning, let none go to work. Let us take the blue sky by storm and plunder space as we run. Laughter floats in the air like foam on the flood. Brothers, let us squander our morning in futile songs.
work: The Gardener, 84 · translated by the author

title: Fruit-Gathering · LXXXIV
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
THE OARSMEN

Do you hear the tumult of death afar, The call midst the fire-floods and poisonous clouds --The Captain's call to the steersman to turn the ship to an unnamed shore, For that time is over--the stagnant time in the port-- Where the same old merchandise is bought and sold in an endless round, Where dead things drift in the exhaustion and emptiness of truth.

They wake up in sudden fear and ask, "Comrades, what hour has struck? When shall the dawn begin?" The clouds have blotted away the stars-- Who is there then can see the beckoning finger of the day? They run out with oars in hand, the beds are emptied, the mother prays, the wife watches by the door; There is a wail of parting that rises to the sky, And there is the Captain's voice in the dark: "Come, sailors, for the time in the harbour is over!"

All the black evils in the world have overflowed their banks, Yet, oarsmen, take your places with the blessing of sorrow in your souls! Whom do you blame, brothers? Bow your heads down! The sin has been yours and ours. The heat growing in the heart of God for ages-- The cowardice of the weak, the arrogance of the strong, the greed of fat prosperity, the rancour of the wronged, pride of race, and insult to man-- Has burst God's peace, raging in storm.

Like a ripe pod, let the tempest break its heart into pieces, scattering thunders. Stop your bluster of dispraise and of self-praise, And with the calm of silent prayer on your foreheads sail to that unnamed shore.

We have known sins and evils every day and death we have known; They pass over our world like clouds mocking us with their transient lightning laughter. Suddenly they have stopped, become a prodigy, And men must stand before them saying: "We do not fear you, O Monster! for we have lived every day by conquering you, "And we die with the faith that Peace is true, and Good is true, and true is the eternal One!"

If the Deathless dwell not in the heart of death, If glad wisdom bloom not bursting the sheath of sorrow, If sin do not die of its own revealment, If pride break not under its load of decorations, Then whence comes the hope that drives these men from their homes like stars rushing to their death in the morning light? Shall the value of the martyrs' blood and mothers' tears be utterly lost in the dust of the earth, not buying Heaven with their price? And when Man bursts his mortal bounds, is not the Boundless revealed that moment?
work: Fruit-Gathering, LXXXIV · translated by the author

title: "Troubled About Many Things."
author: Emily Dickinson
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XI · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 85
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The artist is the lover of Nature, therefore he is her slave and her master.
work: Stray Birds, 85 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 85
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
When the warriors came out first from their master’s hall, where had they hid their power? Where were their armour and their arms?

They looked poor and helpless, and the arrows were showered upon them on the day they came out from their master’s hall.

When the warriors marched back again to their master’s hall where did they hide their power?

They had dropped the sword and dropped the bow and the arrow; peace was on their foreheads, and they had left the fruits of their life behind them on the day they marched back again to their master’s hall.
work: Gitanjali, 85 · translated by the author

title: The Gardener · 85
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Who are you, reader, reading my poems an hundred years hence? I cannot send you one single flower from this wealth of the spring, one single streak of gold from yonder clouds. Open your doors and look abroad. From your blossoming garden gather fragrant memories of the vanished flowers of an hundred years before. In the joy of your heart may you feel the living joy that sang one spring morning, sending its glad voice across an hundred years.
work: The Gardener, 85 · translated by the author

title: Fruit-Gathering · LXXXV
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
THE SONG OF THE DEFEATED

My Master has bid me while I stand at the roadside, to sing the song of Defeat, for that is the bride whom He woos in secret.

She has put on the dark veil, hiding her face from the crowd, but the jewel glows on her breast in the dark.

She is forsaken of the day, and God's night is waiting for her with its lamps lighted and flowers wet with dew.

She is silent with her eyes downcast; she has left her home behind her, from her home has come that wailing in the wind.

But the stars are singing the love-song of the eternal to a face sweet with shame and suffering.

The door has been opened in the lonely chamber, the call has sounded, and the heart of the darkness throbs with awe because of the coming tryst.
work: Fruit-Gathering, LXXXV · translated by the author

title: Real
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I like a look of agony,
Because I know it 's true;
Men do not sham convulsion,
Nor simulate a throe.

The eyes glaze once, and that is death.
Impossible to feign
The beads upon the forehead
By homely anguish strung.
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 86
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
"How far are you from me, O Fruit?"

"I am hidden in your heart, O Flower."
work: Stray Birds, 86 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 86
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
Death, thy servant, is at my door. He has crossed the unknown sea and brought thy call to my home.

The night is dark and my heart is fearful—yet I will take up the lamp, open my gates and bow to him my welcome. It is thy messenger who stands at my door.

I will worship him placing at his feet the treasure of my heart.

He will go back with his errand done, leaving a dark shadow on my morning; and in my desolate home only my forlorn self will remain as my last offering to thee.
work: Gitanjali, 86 · translated by the author

title: Fruit-Gathering · LXXXVI
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
THANKSGIVING

Those who walk on the path of pride crushing the lowly life under their tread, covering the tender green of the earth with their footprints in blood;

Let them rejoice, and thank thee, Lord, for the day is theirs.

But I am thankful that my lot lies with the humble who suffer and bear the burden of power, and hide their faces and stifle their sobs in the dark.

For every throb of their pain has pulsed in the secret depth of thy night, and every insult has been gathered into thy great silence. And the morrow is theirs.

O Sun, rise upon the bleeding hearts blossoming in flowers of the morning, and the torchlight revelry of pride shrunken to ashes.
work: Fruit-Gathering, LXXXVI · translated by the author

title: The Funeral
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
That short, potential stir
That each can make but once,
That bustle so illustrious
'T is almost consequence,

Is the eclat of death.
Oh, thou unknown renown
That not a beggar would accept,
Had he the power to spurn!
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XIII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 87
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: This longing is for the one who is felt in the dark, but not seen in the day.
work: Stray Birds, 87 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 87
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
In desperate hope I go and search for her in all the corners of my room; I find her not.

My house is small and what once has gone from it can never be regained.

But infinite is thy mansion, my lord, and seeking her I have to come to thy door.

I stand under the golden canopy of thine evening sky and I lift my eager eyes to thy face.

I have come to the brink of eternity from which nothing can vanish—no hope, no happiness, no vision of a face seen through tears.

Oh, dip my emptied life into that ocean, plunge it into the deepest fullness. Let me for once feel that lost sweet touch in the allness of the universe.
work: Gitanjali, 87 · translated by the author

title: I went to thank her
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I went to thank her,
But she slept;
Her bed a funnelled stone,
With nosegays at the head and foot,
That travellers had thrown,

Who went to thank her;
But she slept.
'T was short to cross the sea
To look upon her like, alive,
But turning back 't was slow.
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XIV · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 88
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: "You are the big drop of dew under the lotus leaf, I am the smaller one on its upper side," said the dewdrop to the lake.
work: Stray Birds, 88 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 88
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
Deity of the ruined temple! The broken strings of _Vina_ sing no more your praise. The bells in the evening proclaim not your time of worship. The air is still and silent about you.

In your desolate dwelling comes the vagrant spring breeze. It brings the tidings of flowers—the flowers that for your worship are offered no more.

Your worshipper of old wanders ever longing for favour still refused. In the eventide, when fires and shadows mingle with the gloom of dust, he wearily comes back to the ruined temple with hunger in his heart.

Many a festival day comes to you in silence, deity of the ruined temple. Many a night of worship goes away with lamp unlit.

Many new images are built by masters of cunning art and carried to the holy stream of oblivion when their time is come.

Only the deity of the ruined temple remains unworshipped in deathless neglect.
work: Gitanjali, 88 · translated by the author

title: I've seen a dying eye
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I've seen a dying eye
Run round and round a room
In search of something, as it seemed,
Then cloudier become;
And then, obscure with fog,
And then be soldered down,
Without disclosing what it be,
'T were blessed to have seen.
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XV · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 89
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The scabbard is content to be dull when it protects the keenness of the sword.
work: Stray Birds, 89 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 89
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
No more noisy, loud words from me—such is my master’s will. Henceforth I deal in whispers. The speech of my heart will be carried on in murmurings of a song.

Men hasten to the King’s market. All the buyers and sellers are there. But I have my untimely leave in the middle of the day, in the thick of work.

Let then the flowers come out in my garden, though it is not their time; and let the midday bees strike up their lazy hum.

Full many an hour have I spent in the strife of the good and the evil, but now it is the pleasure of my playmate of the empty days to draw my heart on to him; and I know not why is this sudden call to what useless inconsequence!
work: Gitanjali, 89 · translated by the author

title: Refuge
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
The clouds their backs together laid,
The north begun to push,
The forests galloped till they fell,
The lightning skipped like mice;
The thunder crumbled like a stuff --
How good to be safe in tombs,
Where nature's temper cannot reach,
Nor vengeance ever comes!
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XVI · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 90
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: In darkness the One appears as uniform; in the light the One appears as manifold.
work: Stray Birds, 90 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 90
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
On the day when death will knock at thy door what wilt thou offer to him?

Oh, I will set before my guest the full vessel of my life—I will never let him go with empty hands.

All the sweet vintage of all my autumn days and summer nights, all the earnings and gleanings of my busy life will I place before him at the close of my days when death will knock at my door.
work: Gitanjali, 90 · translated by the author

title: I never saw a moor
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I never saw a moor,
I never saw the sea;
Yet know I how the heather looks,
And what a wave must be.

I never spoke with God,
Nor visited in heaven;
Yet certain am I of the spot
As if the chart were given.
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XVII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 91
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The great earth makes herself hospitable with the help of the grass.
work: Stray Birds, 91 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 91
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
O thou the last fulfilment of life, Death, my death, come and whisper to me!

Day after day I have kept watch for thee; for thee have I borne the joys and pangs of life.

All that I am, that I have, that I hope and all my love have ever flowed towards thee in depth of secrecy. One final glance from thine eyes and my life will be ever thine own.

The flowers have been woven and the garland is ready for the bridegroom. After the wedding the bride shall leave her home and meet her lord alone in the solitude of night.
work: Gitanjali, 91 · translated by the author

title: Playmates
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
God permits industrious angels
Afternoons to play.
I met one, -- forgot my school-mates,
All, for him, straightway.

God calls home the angels promptly
At the setting sun;
I missed mine. How dreary marbles,
After playing Crown!
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XVIII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 92
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The birth and death of the leaves are the rapid whirls of the eddy whose wider circles move slowly among stars.
work: Stray Birds, 92 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 92
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
I know that the day will come when my sight of this earth shall be lost, and life will take its leave in silence, drawing the last curtain over my eyes.

Yet stars will watch at night, and morning rise as before, and hours heave like sea waves casting up pleasures and pains.

When I think of this end of my moments, the barrier of the moments breaks and I see by the light of death thy world with its careless treasures. Rare is its lowliest seat, rare is its meanest of lives.

Things that I longed for in vain and things that I got—let them pass. Let me but truly possess the things that I ever spurned and overlooked.
work: Gitanjali, 92 · translated by the author

title: To know just how he suffered would be dear
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
To know just how he suffered would be dear;
To know if any human eyes were near
To whom he could intrust his wavering gaze,
Until it settled firm on Paradise.

To know if he was patient, part content,
Was dying as he thought, or different;
Was it a pleasant day to die,
And did the sunshine face his way?

What was his furthest mind, of home, or God,
Or what the distant say
At news that he ceased human nature
On such a day?

And wishes, had he any?
Just his sigh, accented,
Had been legible to me.
And was he confident until
Ill fluttered out in everlasting well?

And if he spoke, what name was best,
What first,
What one broke off with
At the drowsiest?

Was he afraid, or tranquil?
Might he know
How conscious consciousness could grow,
Till love that was, and love too blest to be,
Meet -- and the junction be Eternity?
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XIX · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 93
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Power said to the world, "You are mine. The world kept it prisoner on her throne. Love said to the world, "I am thine." The world gave it the freedom of her house.
work: Stray Birds, 93 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 93
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
I have got my leave. Bid me farewell, my brothers! I bow to you all and take my departure.

Here I give back the keys of my door—and I give up all claims to my house. I only ask for last kind words from you.

We were neighbours for long, but I received more than I could give. Now the day has dawned and the lamp that lit my dark corner is out. A summons has come and I am ready for my journey.
work: Gitanjali, 93 · translated by the author

title: The last night that she lived
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
The last night that she lived,
It was a common night,
Except the dying; this to us
Made nature different.

We noticed smallest things, --
Things overlooked before,
By this great light upon our minds
Italicized, as 't were.

That others could exist
While she must finish quite,
A jealousy for her arose
So nearly infinite.

We waited while she passed;
It was a narrow time,
Too jostled were our souls to speak,
At length the notice came.

She mentioned, and forgot;
Then lightly as a reed
Bent to the water, shivered scarce,
Consented, and was dead.

And we, we placed the hair,
And drew the head erect;
And then an awful leisure was,
Our faith to regulate.
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XX · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 94
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The mist is like the earth's desire. It hides the sun for whom she cries.
work: Stray Birds, 94 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 94
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
At this time of my parting, wish me good luck, my friends! The sky is flushed with the dawn and my path lies beautiful.

Ask not what I have with me to take there. I start on my journey with empty hands and expectant heart.

I shall put on my wedding garland. Mine is not the red-brown dress of the traveller, and though there are dangers on the way I have no fear in mind.

The evening star will come out when my voyage is done and the plaintive notes of the twilight melodies be struck up from the King’s gateway.
work: Gitanjali, 94 · translated by the author

title: The First Lesson
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Not in this world to see his face
Sounds long, until I read the place
Where this is said to be
But just the primer to a life
Unopened, rare, upon the shelf,
Clasped yet to him and me.

And yet, my primer suits me so
I would not choose a book to know
Than that, be sweeter wise;
Might some one else so learned be,
And leave me just my A B C,
Himself could have the skies.
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXI · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 95
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Be still, my heart, these great trees are prayers.
work: Stray Birds, 95 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 95
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
I was not aware of the moment when I first crossed the threshold of this life.

What was the power that made me open out into this vast mystery like a bud in the forest at midnight!

When in the morning I looked upon the light I felt in a moment that I was no stranger in this world, that the inscrutable without name and form had taken me in its arms in the form of my own mother.

Even so, in death the same unknown will appear as ever known to me. And because I love this life, I know I shall love death as well.

The child cries out when from the right breast the mother takes it away, in the very next moment to find in the left one its consolation.
work: Gitanjali, 95 · translated by the author

title: The bustle in a house
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
The bustle in a house
The morning after death
Is solemnest of industries
Enacted upon earth, --

The sweeping up the heart,
And putting love away
We shall not want to use again
Until eternity.
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 96
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The noise of the moment scoffs at the music of the Eternal.
work: Stray Birds, 96 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 96
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
When I go from hence let this be my parting word, that what I have seen is unsurpassable.

I have tasted of the hidden honey of this lotus that expands on the ocean of light, and thus am I blessed—let this be my parting word.

In this playhouse of infinite forms I have had my play and here have I caught sight of him that is formless.

My whole body and my limbs have thrilled with his touch who is beyond touch; and if the end comes here, let it come—let this be my parting word.
work: Gitanjali, 96 · translated by the author

title: I reason, earth is short
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I reason, earth is short,
And anguish absolute,
And many hurt;
But what of that?

I reason, we could die:
The best vitality
Cannot excel decay;
But what of that?

I reason that in heaven
Somehow, it will be even,
Some new equation given;
But what of that?
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXIII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 97
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: I think of other ages that floated upon the stream of life and love and death and are forgotten, and I feel the freedom of passing away.
work: Stray Birds, 97 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 97
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
When my play was with thee I never questioned who thou wert. I knew nor shyness nor fear, my life was boisterous.

In the early morning thou wouldst call me from my sleep like my own comrade and lead me running from glade to glade.

On those days I never cared to know the meaning of songs thou sangest to me. Only my voice took up the tunes, and my heart danced in their cadence.

Now, when the playtime is over, what is this sudden sight that is come upon me? The world with eyes bent upon thy feet stands in awe with all its silent stars.
work: Gitanjali, 97 · translated by the author

title: Afraid? Of whom am I afraid?
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Afraid? Of whom am I afraid?
Not death; for who is he?
The porter of my father's lodge
As much abasheth me.

Of life? 'T were odd I fear a thing
That comprehendeth me
In one or more existences
At Deity's decree.

Of resurrection? Is the east
Afraid to trust the morn
With her fastidious forehead?
As soon impeach my crown!
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXIV · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 98
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The sadness of my soul is her bride's veil. It waits to be lifted in the night.
work: Stray Birds, 98 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 98
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
I will deck thee with trophies, garlands of my defeat. It is never in my power to escape unconquered.

I surely know my pride will go to the wall, my life will burst its bonds in exceeding pain, and my empty heart will sob out in music like a hollow reed, and the stone will melt in tears.

I surely know the hundred petals of a lotus will not remain closed for ever and the secret recess of its honey will be bared.

From the blue sky an eye shall gaze upon me and summon me in silence. Nothing will be left for me, nothing whatever, and utter death shall I receive at thy feet.
work: Gitanjali, 98 · translated by the author

title: Dying
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
The sun kept setting, setting still;
No hue of afternoon
Upon the village I perceived, --
From house to house 't was noon.

The dusk kept dropping, dropping still;
No dew upon the grass,
But only on my forehead stopped,
And wandered in my face.

My feet kept drowsing, drowsing still,
My fingers were awake;
Yet why so little sound myself
Unto my seeming make?

How well I knew the light before!
I could not see it now.
'T is dying, I am doing; but
I'm not afraid to know.
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXV · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 99
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Death's stamp gives value to the coin of life; making it possible to buy with life what is truly precious.
work: Stray Birds, 99 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 99
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
When I give up the helm I know that the time has come for thee to take it. What there is to do will be instantly done. Vain is this struggle.

Then take away your hands and silently put up with your defeat, my heart, and think it your good fortune to sit perfectly still where you are placed.

These my lamps are blown out at every little puff of wind, and trying to light them I forget all else again and again.

But I shall be wise this time and wait in the dark, spreading my mat on the floor; and whenever it is thy pleasure, my lord, come silently and take thy seat here.
work: Gitanjali, 99 · translated by the author

title: Two swimmers wrestled on the spar
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Two swimmers wrestled on the spar
Until the morning sun,
When one turned smiling to the land.
O God, the other one!

The stray ships passing spied a face
Upon the waters borne,
With eyes in death still begging raised,
And hands beseeching thrown.
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXVI · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 100
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The cloud stood humbly in a corner of the sky. The morning crowned it with splendour.
work: Stray Birds, 100 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 100
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
I dive down into the depth of the ocean of forms, hoping to gain the perfect pearl of the formless.

No more sailing from harbour to harbour with this my weather-beaten boat. The days are long passed when my sport was to be tossed on waves.

And now I am eager to die into the deathless.

Into the audience hall by the fathomless abyss where swells up the music of toneless strings I shall take this harp of my life.

I shall tune it to the notes of forever, and when it has sobbed out its last utterance, lay down my silent harp at the feet of the silent.
work: Gitanjali, 100 · translated by the author

title: The Chariot
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Because I could not stop for Death,
He kindly stopped for me;
The carriage held but just ourselves
And Immortality.

We slowly drove, he knew no haste,
And I had put away
My labor, and my leisure too,
For his civility.

We passed the school where children played,
Their lessons scarcely done;
We passed the fields of gazing grain,
We passed the setting sun.

We paused before a house that seemed
A swelling of the ground;
The roof was scarcely visible,
The cornice but a mound.

Since then 't is centuries; but each
Feels shorter than the day
I first surmised the horses' heads
Were toward eternity.
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXVII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 101
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The dust receives insult and in return offers her flowers.
work: Stray Birds, 101 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 101
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
Ever in my life have I sought thee with my songs. It was they who led me from door to door, and with them have I felt about me, searching and touching my world.

It was my songs that taught me all the lessons I ever learnt; they showed me secret paths, they brought before my sight many a star on the horizon of my heart.

They guided me all the day long to the mysteries of the country of pleasure and pain, and, at last, to what palace gate have they brought me in the evening at the end of my journey?
work: Gitanjali, 101 · translated by the author

title: She went as quiet as the dew
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
She went as quiet as the dew
From a familiar flower.
Not like the dew did she return
At the accustomed hour!

She dropt as softly as a star
From out my summer's eve;
Less skilful than Leverrier
It's sorer to believe!
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXVIII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 102
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Do not linger to gather flowers to keep them, but walk on, for flowers will keep themselves blooming all your way.
work: Stray Birds, 102 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 102
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
I boasted among men that I had known you. They see your pictures in all works of mine. They come and ask me, “Who is he?” I know not how to answer them. I say, “Indeed, I cannot tell.” They blame me and they go away in scorn. And you sit there smiling.

I put my tales of you into lasting songs. The secret gushes out from my heart. They come and ask me, “Tell me all your meanings.” I know not how to answer them. I say, “Ah, who knows what they mean!” They smile and go away in utter scorn. And you sit there smiling.
work: Gitanjali, 102 · translated by the author

title: Resurgam
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
At last to be identified!
At last, the lamps upon thy side,
The rest of life to see!
Past midnight, past the morning star!
Past sunrise! Ah! what leagues there are
Between our feet and day!
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXIX · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 103
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Roots are the branches down in the earth. Branches are roots in the air.
work: Stray Birds, 103 · translated by the author

title: Gitanjali · 103
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
In one salutation to thee, my God, let all my senses spread out and touch this world at thy feet.

Like a rain-cloud of July hung low with its burden of unshed showers let all my mind bend down at thy door in one salutation to thee.

Let all my songs gather together their diverse strains into a single current and flow to a sea of silence in one salutation to thee.

Like a flock of homesick cranes flying night and day back to their mountain nests let all my life take its voyage to its eternal home in one salutation to thee.
work: Gitanjali, 103 · translated by the author

title: Except to heaven, she is nought
author: Emily Dickinson
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXX · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 104
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The music of the far-away summer flutters around the Autumn seeking its former nest.
work: Stray Birds, 104 · translated by the author

title: Death is a dialogue between
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Death is a dialogue between
The spirit and the dust.
"Dissolve," says Death. The Spirit, "Sir,
I have another trust."

Death doubts it, argues from the ground.
The Spirit turns away,
Just laying off, for evidence,
An overcoat of clay.
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXXI · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 105
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Do not insult your friend by lending him merits from your own pocket.
work: Stray Birds, 105 · translated by the author

title: It was too late for man
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
It was too late for man,
But early yet for God;
Creation impotent to help,
But prayer remained our side.

How excellent the heaven,
When earth cannot be had;
How hospitable, then, the face
Of our old neighbor, God!
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXXII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 106
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The touch of the nameless days clings to my heart like mosses round the old tree.
work: Stray Birds, 106 · translated by the author

title: Along The Potomac
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
When I was small, a woman died.
To-day her only boy
Went up from the Potomac,
His face all victory,

To look at her; how slowly
The seasons must have turned
Till bullets clipt an angle,
And he passed quickly round!

If pride shall be in Paradise
I never can decide;
Of their imperial conduct,
No person testified.

But proud in apparition,
That woman and her boy
Pass back and forth before my brain,
As ever in the sky.
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXXIII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 107
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The echo mocks her origin to prove she is the original.
work: Stray Birds, 107 · translated by the author

title: The daisy follows soft the sun
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
The daisy follows soft the sun,
And when his golden walk is done,
   Sits shyly at his feet.
He, waking, finds the flower near.
"Wherefore, marauder, art thou here?"
   "Because, sir, love is sweet!"

We are the flower, Thou the sun!
Forgive us, if as days decline,
   We nearer steal to Thee, --
Enamoured of the parting west,
The peace, the flight, the amethyst,
   Night's possibility!
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXXIV · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 108
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: God is ashamed when the prosperous boasts of His special favour.
work: Stray Birds, 108 · translated by the author

title: Emancipation
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
No rack can torture me,
My soul's at liberty
Behind this mortal bone
There knits a bolder one

You cannot prick with saw,
Nor rend with scymitar.
Two bodies therefore be;
Bind one, and one will flee.

The eagle of his nest
No easier divest
And gain the sky,
Than mayest thou,

Except thyself may be
Thine enemy;
Captivity is consciousness,
So's liberty.
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXXV · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 109
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: I cast my own shadow upon my path, because I have a lamp that has not been lighted.
work: Stray Birds, 109 · translated by the author

title: Lost
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I lost a world the other day.
Has anybody found?
You'll know it by the row of stars
Around its forehead bound.

A rich man might not notice it;
Yet to my frugal eye
Of more esteem than ducats.
Oh, find it, sir, for me!
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXXVI · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 110
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Man goes into the noisy crowd to drown his own clamour of silence.
work: Stray Birds, 110 · translated by the author

title: If I shouldn't be alive
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
If I shouldn't be alive
When the robins come,
Give the one in red cravat
A memorial crumb.

If I couldn't thank you,
Being just asleep,
You will know I'm trying
With my granite lip!
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXXVII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 111
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: That which ends in exhaustion is death, but the perfect ending is in the endless.
work: Stray Birds, 111 · translated by the author

title: Sleep is supposed to be
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Sleep is supposed to be,
By souls of sanity,
The shutting of the eye.

Sleep is the station grand
Down which on either hand
The hosts of witness stand!

Morn is supposed to be,
By people of degree,
The breaking of the day.

Morning has not occurred!
That shall aurora be
East of eternity;

One with the banner gay,
One in the red array, --
That is the break of day.
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXXVIII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 112
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The sun has his simple robe of light. The clouds are decked with gorgeousness.
work: Stray Birds, 112 · translated by the author

title: I shall know why, when time is over
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I shall know why, when time is over,
And I have ceased to wonder why;
Christ will explain each separate anguish
In the fair schoolroom of the sky.

He will tell me what Peter promised,
And I, for wonder at his woe,
I shall forget the drop of anguish
That scalds me now, that scalds me now.
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XXXIX · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 113
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The hills are like shouts of children who raise their arms, trying to catch stars.
work: Stray Birds, 113 · translated by the author

title: I never lost as much but twice
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I never lost as much but twice,
And that was in the sod;
Twice have I stood a beggar
Before the door of God!

Angels, twice descending,
Reimbursed my store.
Burglar, banker, father,
I am poor once more!
work: Poems · Series 1 · IV. TIME AND ETERNITY · XL · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 114
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The road is lonely in its crowd for it is not loved.
work: Stray Birds, 114 · translated by the author

title: I'm nobody!  Who are you?
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I'm nobody!  Who are you?
Are you nobody, too?
Then there 's a pair of us -- don't tell!
They 'd banish us, you know.

How dreary to be somebody!
How public, like a frog
To tell your name the livelong day
To an admiring bog!
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · I · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 115
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The power that boasts of its mischiefs is laughed at by the yellow leaves that fall, and clouds that pass by.
work: Stray Birds, 115 · translated by the author

title: I bring an unaccustomed wine
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I bring an unaccustomed wine
To lips long parching, next to mine,
And summon them to drink.

Crackling with fever, they essay;
I turn my brimming eyes away,
And come next hour to look.

The hands still hug the tardy glass;
The lips I would have cooled, alas!
Are so superfluous cold,

I would as soon attempt to warm
The bosoms where the frost has lain
Ages beneath the mould.

Some other thirsty there may be
To whom this would have pointed me
Had it remained to speak.

And so I always bear the cup
If, haply, mine may be the drop
Some pilgrim thirst to slake, --

If, haply, any say to me,
"Unto the little, unto me,"
When I at last awake.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · II · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 116
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The earth hums to me to-day in the sun, like a woman at her spinng, some ballad of the ancient time in a forgotten tongue.
work: Stray Birds, 116 · translated by the author

title: The nearest dream recedes, unrealized
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
The nearest dream recedes, unrealized.
      The heaven we chase
      Like the June bee
      Before the school-boy
      Invites the race;
      Stoops to an easy clover --
Dips -- evades -- teases -- deploys;
      Then to the royal clouds
      Lifts his light pinnace
      Heedless of the boy
Staring, bewildered, at the mocking sky.

      Homesick for steadfast honey,
      Ah! the bee flies not
That brews that rare variety.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · III · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 117
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The grass-blade is worth of the great world where it grows.
work: Stray Birds, 117 · translated by the author

title: We play at paste
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
We play at paste,
Till qualified for pearl,
Then drop the paste,
And deem ourself a fool.
The shapes, though, were similar,
And our new hands
Learned gem-tactics
Practising sands.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · IV · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 118
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Dream is a wife who must talk. Sleep is a husband who silently suffers.
work: Stray Birds, 118 · translated by the author

title: I found the phrase to every thought
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I found the phrase to every thought
I ever had, but one;
And that defies me, -- as a hand
Did try to chalk the sun

To races nurtured in the dark; --
How would your own begin?
Can blaze be done in cochineal,
Or noon in mazarin?
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · V · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 119
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The night kisses the fading day whispering to his ear, "I am death, your mother. I am to give you fresh birth."
work: Stray Birds, 119 · translated by the author

title: Hope
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Hope is the thing with feathers
That perches in the soul,
And sings the tune without the words,
And never stops at all,

And sweetest in the gale is heard;
And sore must be the storm
That could abash the little bird
That kept so many warm.

I 've heard it in the chillest land,
And on the strangest sea;
Yet, never, in extremity,
It asked a crumb of me.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · VI · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 120
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: I feel, thy beauty, dark night, like that of the loved woman when she has put out the lamp.
work: Stray Birds, 120 · translated by the author

title: The White Heat
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Dare you see a soul at the white heat?
   Then crouch within the door.
Red is the fire's common tint;
   But when the vivid ore

Has sated flame's conditions,
   Its quivering substance plays
Without a color but the light
   Of unanointed blaze.

Least village boasts its blacksmith,
   Whose anvil's even din
Stands symbol for the finer forge
   That soundless tugs within,

Refining these impatient ores
   With hammer and with blaze,
Until the designated light
   Repudiate the forge.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · VII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 121
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: I carry in my world that flourishes the worlds that have failed.
work: Stray Birds, 121 · translated by the author

title: Triumphant
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Who never lost, are unprepared
A coronet to find;
Who never thirsted, flagons
And cooling tamarind.

Who never climbed the weary league --
Can such a foot explore
The purple territories
On Pizarro's shore?

How many legions overcome?
The emperor will say.
How many colors taken
On Revolution Day?

How many bullets bearest?
The royal scar hast thou?
Angels, write "Promoted"
On this soldier's brow!
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · VIII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 122
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Dear friend, I feel the silence of your great thoughts of may a deepening eventide on this beach when I listen to these waves.
work: Stray Birds, 122 · translated by the author

title: The Test
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I can wade grief,
Whole pools of it, --
I 'm used to that.
But the least push of joy
Breaks up my feet,
And I tip -- drunken.
Let no pebble smile,
'T was the new liquor, --
That was all!

Power is only pain,
Stranded, through discipline,
Till weights will hang.
Give balm to giants,
And they 'll wilt, like men.
Give Himmaleh, --
They 'll carry him!
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · IX · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 123
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The bird thinks it is an act of kindness to give the fish a lift in the air.
work: Stray Birds, 123 · translated by the author

title: Escape
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I never hear the word "escape"
Without a quicker blood,
A sudden expectation,
A flying attitude.

I never hear of prisons broad
By soldiers battered down,
But I tug childish at my bars, --
Only to fail again!
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · X · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 124
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
"In the moon thou sendest thy love letters to me," said the night to the sun.

"I leave my answers in tears upon the grass."
work: Stray Birds, 124 · translated by the author

title: Compensation
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
For each ecstatic instant
We must an anguish pay
In keen and quivering ratio
To the ecstasy.

For each beloved hour
Sharp pittances of years,
Bitter contested farthings
And coffers heaped with tears.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XI · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 125
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The Great is a born child; when he dies he gives his great childhood to the world.
work: Stray Birds, 125 · translated by the author

title: The Martyrs
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Through the straight pass of suffering
The martyrs even trod,
Their feet upon temptation,
Their faces upon God.

A stately, shriven company;
Convulsion playing round,
Harmless as streaks of meteor
Upon a planet's bound.

Their faith the everlasting troth;
Their expectation fair;
The needle to the north degree
Wades so, through polar air.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 126
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Not hammerstrokes, but dance of the water sings the pebbles into perfection.
work: Stray Birds, 126 · translated by the author

title: A Prayer
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I meant to have but modest needs,
Such as content, and heaven;
Within my income these could lie,
And life and I keep even.

But since the last included both,
It would suffice my prayer
But just for one to stipulate,
And grace would grant the pair.

And so, upon this wise I prayed, --
Great Spirit, give to me
A heaven not so large as yours,
But large enough for me.

A smile suffused Jehovah's face;
The cherubim withdrew;
Grave saints stole out to look at me,
And showed their dimples, too.

I left the place with all my might, --
My prayer away I threw;
The quiet ages picked it up,
And Judgment twinkled, too,

That one so honest be extant
As take the tale for true
That "Whatsoever you shall ask,
Itself be given you."

But I, grown shrewder, scan the skies
With a suspicious air, --
As children, swindled for the first,
All swindlers be, infer.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XIII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 127
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Bees sip honey from flowers and hum their thanks when they leave. The gaudy butterfly is sure that the flowers owe thanks to him.
work: Stray Birds, 127 · translated by the author

title: The thought beneath so slight a film
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
The thought beneath so slight a film
Is more distinctly seen, --
As laces just reveal the surge,
Or mists the Apennine.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XIV · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 128
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: To be outspoken is easy when you do not wait to speak the complete truth.
work: Stray Birds, 128 · translated by the author

title: The soul unto itself
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
The soul unto itself
Is an imperial friend, --
Or the most agonizing spy
An enemy could send.

Secure against its own,
No treason it can fear;
Itself its sovereign, of itself
The soul should stand in awe.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XV · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 129
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
Asks the Possible to the Impossible, "Where is your dwelling place?"

"In the dreams of the impotent," comes the answer.
work: Stray Birds, 129 · translated by the author

title: Surgeons must be very careful
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Surgeons must be very careful
When they take the knife!
Underneath their fine incisions
Stirs the culprit, -- Life!
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XVI · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 130
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: If you shut your door to all errors truth will be shut out.
work: Stray Birds, 130 · translated by the author

title: The Railway Train
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I like to see it lap the miles,
And lick the valleys up,
And stop to feed itself at tanks;
And then, prodigious, step

Around a pile of mountains,
And, supercilious, peer
In shanties by the sides of roads;
And then a quarry pare

To fit its sides, and crawl between,
Complaining all the while
In horrid, hooting stanza;
Then chase itself down hill

And neigh like Boanerges;
Then, punctual as a star,
Stop -- docile and omnipotent --
At its own stable door.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XVII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 131
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: I hear some rustle of things behind my sadness of heart,--I cannot see them.
work: Stray Birds, 131 · translated by the author

title: The Show
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
The show is not the show,
But they that go.
Menagerie to me
My neighbor be.
Fair play --
Both went to see.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XVIII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 132
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Leisure in its activity is work. The stillness of the sea stirs in waves.
work: Stray Birds, 132 · translated by the author

title: Delight becomes pictorial
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Delight becomes pictorial
When viewed through pain, --
More fair, because impossible
That any gain.

The mountain at a given distance
In amber lies;
Approached, the amber flits a little, --
And that 's the skies!
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XIX · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 133
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The leaf becomes flower when it loves. The flower becomes fruit when it worships.
work: Stray Birds, 133 · translated by the author

title: A thought went up my mind to-day
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
A thought went up my mind to-day
That I have had before,
But did not finish, -- some way back,
I could not fix the year,

Nor where it went, nor why it came
The second time to me,
Nor definitely what it was,
Have I the art to say.

But somewhere in my soul, I know
I 've met the thing before;
It just reminded me -- 't was all --
And came my way no more.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XX · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 134
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The roots below the earth claim no rewards for making the branches fruitful.
work: Stray Birds, 134 · translated by the author

title: Is Heaven a physician?
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Is Heaven a physician?
They say that He can heal,
But medicine posthumous
   Is unavailable.

Is Heaven an exchequer?
   They speak of what we owe;
But that negotiation
   I 'm not a party to.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXI · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 135
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: This rainy evening the wind is restless. I look at the swaying branches and ponder over the greatness of all things.
work: Stray Birds, 135 · translated by the author

title: The Return
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Though I get home how late, how late!
So I get home, 't will compensate.
Better will be the ecstasy
That they have done expecting me,
When, night descending, dumb and dark,
They hear my unexpected knock.
Transporting must the moment be,
Brewed from decades of agony!

To think just how the fire will burn,
Just how long-cheated eyes will turn
To wonder what myself will say,
And what itself will say to me,
Beguiles the centuries of way!
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 136
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Storm of midnight, like a giant child awakened in the untimely dark, has begun to play and shout.
work: Stray Birds, 136 · translated by the author

title: A poor torn heart, a tattered heart
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
A poor torn heart, a tattered heart,
That sat it down to rest,
Nor noticed that the ebbing day
Flowed silver to the west,
Nor noticed night did soft descend
Nor constellation burn,
Intent upon the vision
Of latitudes unknown.

The angels, happening that way,
This dusty heart espied;
Tenderly took it up from toil
And carried it to God.
There, -- sandals for the barefoot;
There, -- gathered from the gales,
Do the blue havens by the hand
Lead the wandering sails.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXIII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 137
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Thou raisest thy waves vainly to follow thy lover. O sea, thou lonely bride of the storm.
work: Stray Birds, 137 · translated by the author

title: Too Much
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I should have been too glad, I see,
Too lifted for the scant degree
   Of life's penurious round;
My little circuit would have shamed
This new circumference, have blamed
   The homelier time behind.

I should have been too saved, I see,
Too rescued; fear too dim to me
   That I could spell the prayer
I knew so perfect yesterday, --
That scalding one, "Sabachthani,"
   Recited fluent here.

Earth would have been too much, I see,
And heaven not enough for me;
   I should have had the joy
Without the fear to justify, --
The palm without the Calvary;
   So, Saviour, crucify.

Defeat whets victory, they say;
The reefs in old Gethsemane
   Endear the shore beyond.
'T is beggars banquets best define;
'T is thirsting vitalizes wine, --
   Faith faints to understand.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXIV · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 138
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: "I am ashamed of my emptiness," said the Word to the Work. "I know how poor I am when I see you," said the Work to the Word.
work: Stray Birds, 138 · translated by the author

title: Shipwreck
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
It tossed and tossed, --
A little brig I knew, --
O'ertook by blast,
It spun and spun,
And groped delirious, for morn.

It slipped and slipped,
As one that drunken stepped;
Its white foot tripped,
Then dropped from sight.

Ah, brig, good-night
To crew and you;
The ocean's heart too smooth, too blue,
To break for you.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXV · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 139
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Time is the wealth of change, but the clock in its parody makes it mere change and no wealth.
work: Stray Birds, 139 · translated by the author

title: Victory comes late
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Victory comes late,
And is held low to freezing lips
Too rapt with frost
To take it.
How sweet it would have tasted,
Just a drop!
Was God so economical?
His table 's spread too high for us
Unless we dine on tip-toe.
Crumbs fit such little mouths,
Cherries suit robins;
The eagle's golden breakfast
Strangles them.
God keeps his oath to sparrows,
Who of little love
Know how to starve!
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXVI · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 140
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Truth in her dress finds facts too tight. In fiction she moves with ease.
work: Stray Birds, 140 · translated by the author

title: Enough
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
God gave a loaf to every bird,
But just a crumb to me;
I dare not eat it, though I starve, --
My poignant luxury
To own it, touch it, prove the feat
That made the pellet mine, --
Too happy in my sparrow chance
For ampler coveting.

It might be famine all around,
I could not miss an ear,
Such plenty smiles upon my board,
My garner shows so fair.
I wonder how the rich may feel, --
An Indiaman -- an Earl?
I deem that I with but a crumb
Am sovereign of them all.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXVII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 141
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: When I travelled to here and to there, I was tired of thee, O Road, but now when thou leadest me to everywhere I am wedded to thee in love.
work: Stray Birds, 141 · translated by the author

title: Experiment to me
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Experiment to me
Is every one I meet.
If it contain a kernel?
The figure of a nut

Presents upon a tree,
Equally plausibly;
But meat within is requisite,
To squirrels and to me.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXVIII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 142
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Let me think that there is one among those stars that guides my life through the dark unknown.
work: Stray Birds, 142 · translated by the author

title: My Country'S Wardrobe
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
My country need not change her gown,
Her triple suit as sweet
As when 't was cut at Lexington,
And first pronounced "a fit."

Great Britain disapproves "the stars;"
Disparagement discreet, --
There 's something in their attitude
That taunts her bayonet.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXIX · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 143
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Woman, with the grace of your fingers you touched my things and order came out like music.
work: Stray Birds, 143 · translated by the author

title: Faith is a fine invention
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Faith is a fine invention
For gentlemen who see;
But microscopes are prudent
In an emergency!
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXX · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 144
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: One sad voice has its nest among the ruins of the years. It sings to me in the night,--"I loved you."
work: Stray Birds, 144 · translated by the author

title: Except the heaven had come so near
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Except the heaven had come so near,
So seemed to choose my door,
The distance would not haunt me so;
I had not hoped before.

But just to hear the grace depart
I never thought to see,
Afflicts me with a double loss;
'T is lost, and lost to me.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXXI · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 145
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The flaming fire warns me off by its own glow. Save me from the dying embers hidden under ashes.
work: Stray Birds, 145 · translated by the author

title: Portraits are to daily faces
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Portraits are to daily faces
As an evening west
To a fine, pedantic sunshine
In a satin vest.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXXII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 146
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: I have my stars in the sky, But oh for my little lamp unlit in my house.
work: Stray Birds, 146 · translated by the author

title: The Duel
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I took my power in my hand.
And went against the world;
'T was not so much as David had,
But I was twice as bold.

I aimed my pebble, but myself
Was all the one that fell.
Was it Goliath was too large,
Or only I too small?
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXXIII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 147
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The dust of the dead words clings to thee. Wash thy soul with silence.
work: Stray Birds, 147 · translated by the author

title: A shady friend for torrid days
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
A shady friend for torrid days
Is easier to find
Than one of higher temperature
For frigid hour of mind.

The vane a little to the east
Scares muslin souls away;
If broadcloth breasts are firmer
Than those of organdy,

Who is to blame? The weaver?
Ah! the bewildering thread!
The tapestries of paradise
So notelessly are made!
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXXIV · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 148
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Gaps are left in life through which comes the sad music of death.
work: Stray Birds, 148 · translated by the author

title: The Goal
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Each life converges to some centre
Expressed or still;
Exists in every human nature
A goal,

Admitted scarcely to itself, it may be,
Too fair
For credibility's temerity
To dare.

Adored with caution, as a brittle heaven,
To reach
Were hopeless as the rainbow's raiment
To touch,

Yet persevered toward, surer for the distance;
How high
Unto the saints' slow diligence
The sky!

Ungained, it may be, by a life's low venture,
But then,
Eternity enables the endeavoring
Again.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXXV · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 149
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The world has opened its heart of light in the morning. Come out, my heart, with thy love to meet it.
work: Stray Birds, 149 · translated by the author

title: Sight
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Before I got my eye put out,
I liked as well to see
As other creatures that have eyes,
And know no other way.

But were it told to me, to-day,
That I might have the sky
For mine, I tell you that my heart
Would split, for size of me.

The meadows mine, the mountains mine, --
All forests, stintless stars,
As much of noon as I could take
Between my finite eyes.

The motions of the dipping birds,
The lightning's jointed road,
For mine to look at when I liked, --
The news would strike me dead!

So safer, guess, with just my soul
Upon the window-pane
Where other creatures put their eyes,
Incautious of the sun.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXXVI · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 150
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: My thoughts shimmer with these shimmering leaves and my heart sings with the touch of this sunlight; my life is glad to be floating with all things into the blue of space, into the dark of time.
work: Stray Birds, 150 · translated by the author

title: Talk with prudence to a beggar
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Talk with prudence to a beggar
Of 'Potosi' and the mines!
Reverently to the hungry
Of your viands and your wines!

Cautious, hint to any captive
You have passed enfranchised feet!
Anecdotes of air in dungeons
Have sometimes proved deadly sweet!
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXXVII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 151
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: God's great power is in the gentle breeze, not in the storm.
work: Stray Birds, 151 · translated by the author

title: The Preacher
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
He preached upon "breadth" till it argued him narrow, --
The broad are too broad to define;
And of "truth" until it proclaimed him a liar, --
The truth never flaunted a sign.

Simplicity fled from his counterfeit presence
As gold the pyrites would shun.
What confusion would cover the innocent Jesus
To meet so enabled a man!
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXXVIII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 152
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: This is a dream in which things are all loose and they oppress. I shall find them gathered in thee when I awake and shall be free.
work: Stray Birds, 152 · translated by the author

title: Good night! which put the candle out?
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Good night! which put the candle out?
A jealous zephyr, not a doubt.
   Ah! friend, you little knew
How long at that celestial wick
The angels labored diligent;
   Extinguished, now, for you!

It might have been the lighthouse spark
Some sailor, rowing in the dark,
   Had importuned to see!
It might have been the waning lamp
That lit the drummer from the camp
   To purer reveille!
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XXXIX · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 153
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
"Who is there to take up my duties?" asked the setting sun.

"I shall do what I can, my Master," said the earthen lamp.
work: Stray Birds, 153 · translated by the author

title: When I hoped I feared
author: Emily Dickinson
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XL · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 154
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: By plucking her petals you do not gather the beauty of the flower.
work: Stray Birds, 154 · translated by the author

title: Deed
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
A deed knocks first at thought,
And then it knocks at will.
That is the manufacturing spot,
And will at home and well.

It then goes out an act,
Or is entombed so still
That only to the ear of God
Its doom is audible.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XLI · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 155
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Silence will carry your voice like the nest that holds the sleeping birds.
work: Stray Birds, 155 · translated by the author

title: Time'S Lesson
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Mine enemy is growing old, --
I have at last revenge.
The palate of the hate departs;
If any would avenge, --

Let him be quick, the viand flits,
It is a faded meat.
Anger as soon as fed is dead;
'T is starving makes it fat.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XLII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 156
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The Great walks with the Small without fear. The Middling keeps aloof.
work: Stray Birds, 156 · translated by the author

title: Remorse
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Remorse is memory awake,
Her companies astir, --
A presence of departed acts
At window and at door.

It's past set down before the soul,
And lighted with a match,
Perusal to facilitate
Of its condensed despatch.

Remorse is cureless, -- the disease
Not even God can heal;
For 't is his institution, --
The complement of hell.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XLIII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 157
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The night opens the flowers in secret and allows the day to get thanks.
work: Stray Birds, 157 · translated by the author

title: The Shelter
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
The body grows outside, --
The more convenient way, --
That if the spirit like to hide,
Its temple stands alway

Ajar, secure, inviting;
It never did betray
The soul that asked its shelter
In timid honesty.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XLIV · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 158
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Power takes as ingratitude the writhings of its victims.
work: Stray Birds, 158 · translated by the author

title: Undue significance a starving man attaches
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Undue significance a starving man attaches
To food
Far off; he sighs, and therefore hopeless,
And therefore good.

Partaken, it relieves indeed, but proves us
That spices fly
In the receipt. It was the distance
Was savory.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XLV · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 159
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: When we rejoice in our fulness, then we can part with our fruits with joy.
work: Stray Birds, 159 · translated by the author

title: Heart not so heavy as mine
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Heart not so heavy as mine,
Wending late home,
As it passed my window
Whistled itself a tune, --

A careless snatch, a ballad,
A ditty of the street;
Yet to my irritated ear
An anodyne so sweet,

It was as if a bobolink,
Sauntering this way,
Carolled and mused and carolled,
Then bubbled slow away.

It was as if a chirping brook
Upon a toilsome way
Set bleeding feet to minuets
Without the knowing why.

To-morrow, night will come again,
Weary, perhaps, and sore.
Ah, bugle, by my window,
I pray you stroll once more!
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XLVI · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 160
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The raindrops kissed the earth and whispered,--"We are thy homesick children, mother, come back to thee from the heaven."
work: Stray Birds, 160 · translated by the author

title: I many times thought peace had come
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I many times thought peace had come,
When peace was far away;
As wrecked men deem they sight the land
At centre of the sea,

And struggle slacker, but to prove,
As hopelessly as I,
How many the fictitious shores
Before the harbor lie.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XLVII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 161
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The cobweb pretends to catch dew-drops and catches flies.
work: Stray Birds, 161 · translated by the author

title: Unto my books so good to turn
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
Unto my books so good to turn
Far ends of tired days;
It half endears the abstinence,
And pain is missed in praise.

As flavors cheer retarded guests
With banquetings to be,
So spices stimulate the time
Till my small library.

It may be wilderness without,
Far feet of failing men,
But holiday excludes the night,
And it is bells within.

I thank these kinsmen of the shelf;
Their countenances bland
Enamour in prospective,
And satisfy, obtained.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XLVIII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 162
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Love! when you come with the burning lamp of pain in your hand, I can see your face and know you as bliss.
work: Stray Birds, 162 · translated by the author

title: This merit hath the worst
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
This merit hath the worst, --
It cannot be again.
When Fate hath taunted last
And thrown her furthest stone,

The maimed may pause and breathe,
And glance securely round.
The deer invites no longer
Than it eludes the hound.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · XLIX · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 163
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body:
"The learned say that your lights will one day be no more." said the firefly to the stars.

The stars made no answer.
work: Stray Birds, 163 · translated by the author

title: Hunger
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I had been hungry all the years;
My noon had come, to dine;
I, trembling, drew the table near,
And touched the curious wine.

'T was this on tables I had seen,
When turning, hungry, lone,
I looked in windows, for the wealth
I could not hope to own.

I did not know the ample bread,
'T was so unlike the crumb
The birds and I had often shared
In Nature's dining-room.

The plenty hurt me, 't was so new, --
Myself felt ill and odd,
As berry of a mountain bush
Transplanted to the road.

Nor was I hungry; so I found
That hunger was a way
Of persons outside windows,
The entering takes away.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · L · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 164
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: In the dusk of the evening the bird of some early dawn comes to the nest of my silence.
work: Stray Birds, 164 · translated by the author

title: I gained it so
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I gained it so,
      By climbing slow,
By catching at the twigs that grow
Between the bliss and me.
      It hung so high,
      As well the sky
      Attempt by strategy.

I said I gained it, --
      This was all.
Look, how I clutch it,
      Lest it fall,
And I a pauper go;
Unfitted by an instant's grace
For the contented beggar's face
I wore an hour ago.
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · LI · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 165
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: Thoughts pass in my mind like flocks of ducks in the sky. I hear the voice of their wings.
work: Stray Birds, 165 · translated by the author

title: To learn the transport by the pain
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
To learn the transport by the pain,
As blind men learn the sun;
To die of thirst, suspecting
That brooks in meadows run;

To stay the homesick, homesick feet
Upon a foreign shore
Haunted by native lands, the while,
And blue, beloved air --

This is the sovereign anguish,
This, the signal woe!
These are the patient laureates
Whose voices, trained below,

Ascend in ceaseless carol,
Inaudible, indeed,
To us, the duller scholars
Of the mysterious bard!
work: Poems · Series 2 · I. LIFE · LII · early edited text

title: Stray Birds · 166
author: Rabindranath Tagore
body: The canal loves to think that rivers exist solely to supply it with water.
work: Stray Birds, 166 · translated by the author

title: Returning
author: Emily Dickinson
body:
I years had been from home,
And now, before the door,
